strengths: Originality and significance: Organizing nonlinear readouts, selective memory, associative storage, multiscale representations, and predictive geometry around explicit polynomial states is a useful conceptual contribution. The value lies primarily in making memory mechanisms inspectable rather than introducing entirely new capabilities.

Soundness: The salience time-change argument and induced history measure in Equations (2)–(5) provide a clear mathematical interpretation of adaptive memory. The minimum-change associative write update and forecast-induced metric Q = TᵀWT also have straightforward mathematical foundations.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable, and Figures 1–5 connect equations to concrete visualizations of kernels, memory allocation, addresses, and predictive histories. The synthetic experiments are useful demonstrations of task-aligned mechanisms.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly reports poor language-modeling performance, computational trade-offs, and the equivalence of multiscale dynamics to a bank of fixed-scale systems. These disclosures are valuable. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—incorrect foundational dynamics: The Leg-T matrix in Table 2 does not maintain the stated Legendre coefficients. For example, with constant unit input, its first two rows imply steady-state coefficients s₀ = 1 and s₁ = 2/√3, whereas projection of a constant onto the stated orthonormal basis requires s₁ = 0. This directly threatens the explicit-memory interpretation in experiments using Leg-T. The authors need to correct the matrix, identify what was implemented, and verify the affected results.

Soundness—finite-dimensional projection is treated as exact: Appendix D.1 asserts gℓ(g) = Cℓ(g) for a truncated polynomial vector, although multiplication generates a degree outside that span. More importantly, Appendix D.3 identifies the projected multiplication operator for exp(u) with exp(J). For a finite Jacobi truncation these are generally different: projection and matrix exponentiation do not commute. The construction may be a useful approximation, but its approximation scheme, error, and consequences for queried memories are not established.

Significance and evaluation—multiscale efficiency is not demonstrated: Appendix C.4 gives Multiscale HiPPO 16 × 128 = 2,048 state coefficients, versus 16 per single-scale comparator. Figure 4 therefore does not establish parsimonious coverage under comparable memory budgets. A matched-budget bank of log-spaced HiPPO systems is especially important because Appendix D.4 acknowledges the bank equivalence. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent, despite the implementation using a vectorized, exactly discretized system.

Evaluation—baseline comparisons do not adequately support the broader claims: The selective-copying and associative-recall episodes contain only 30 and 12 timesteps, respectively, with no length-generalization study. Mamba is omitted from these comparisons despite motivating the selective-memory claim. Appendix C.6 shows that two-layer Transformers with positional embeddings can reach 98.9–99.7% associative-recall accuracy, making their omission from the main comparison consequential. Matching trainable parameters also does not match recurrent-state capacity. The experiments support specialized demonstrations more convincingly than general conclusions about memory efficiency or competing architectures.

Originality—connections to established methods need deeper treatment: The associative update is a normalized delta-rule update with polynomial key features, yet fast-weight and delta-rule memory methods are not substantively discussed or compared. Similarly, polynomial Volterra readouts and reduced-rank forecasting have established foundations. The paper should distinguish its new understanding from these existing constructions and show what the polynomial formulation adds beyond a change of features or coordinates.

Reproducibility and presentation: Several consequential details are missing or inconsistent. Section 3.2 specifies Leg-T for selective copying, while Appendix C.2 specifies Leg-S. Appendix C.5 does not specify the forecasting rank d or give an explicit predictive-memory projector, and Appendix E does not provide the promised complete reduced-rank construction. Appendix C.3 specifies 12 possible value tokens, while the main text calls approximately 33% chance accuracy without explaining the discrepancy. Tables 1 and 4 lack variability across training seeds. These issues make the reported results difficult to reproduce and interpret reliably.

Evidence for predictive-memory claims remains limited: Figure 5 presents illustrative trajectories and eigenfunctions without aggregate held-out forecasting errors or sensitivity analyses. Training uses an approximate delayed signal from System 1, whereas inference drives System 3 with the true current signal; the resulting representation mismatch is not quantified. The geometric visualization is interesting, but the evidence does not yet establish reliable forecasting behavior or robustness of the inferred memory structure.

strengths: Originality and significance: Organizing five memory mechanisms around explicit polynomial representations provides a useful conceptual perspective. The salience-induced history measure in Eq. (5) and forecasting geometry Q = TᵀWT offer concrete ways to inspect memory allocation and predictive relevance.

Soundness: The time-reparameterization argument and minimum-norm associative write update are well motivated. Synthetic experiments demonstrate task-aligned capabilities, including 100% reported accuracy for salience on selective copying and associative memory on associative recall.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript is generally readable, with informative visualizations and substantial experimental appendices. It candidly reports poor language-modeling transfer and computational trade-offs. These disclosures are appropriate, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—incorrect foundational dynamics: Table 2's Leg-T matrix does not maintain the stated uniform-window Legendre coefficients. For constant input f = 1, its first two rows give stationary coefficients s₀ = 1 and s₁ = 2√3/3, whereas the degree-one coefficient of a constant must be zero. This directly undermines the claimed coefficient interpretation for experiments using this system. The authors must establish whether the error is confined to the table or also affects implementations, and distinguish exact projections from finite-dimensional boundary approximations.

Soundness—multiscale derivation treats approximations as identities: Appendix D.1 asserts gℓ(g) = Cℓ(g) for a finite polynomial basis, although multiplication introduces an omitted higher-degree term. Similarly, exp(J) in Appendix D.3 is generally not the exact finite Galerkin matrix for multiplication by exp(u). These can define useful approximations, but their interpretation requires a truncation analysis or numerical validation that is absent.

Significance—multiscale efficiency is not established: Appendix C.4 gives Multiscale HiPPO 16 × 128 = 2,048 state coefficients, versus 16 for each single-scale baseline, or 64 across the entire four-system bank. This comparison cannot substantiate the claimed parsimonious representation. Appendix D.4 explicitly acknowledges equivalence to a bank of independent systems after diagonalization, making comparison with an equally sized, appropriately spaced bank particularly necessary. Runtime and memory measurements are also missing.

Evaluation—the strongest task comparisons omit essential controls: Mamba is discussed throughout but is absent from the selective-copying and associative-recall comparisons. An explicit delta-rule or fast-weight memory baseline would help isolate the benefit of polynomial addressing. The main Transformer comparisons omit positional embeddings, while Table 3 shows that a two-layer, 27k-parameter Transformer with positional embeddings and additional training reaches 99.7%. These results do not justify broad claims that competing models cannot bind arbitrary key–value pairs. Matching trainable parameters also does not match recurrent-state memory or compute.

Reproducibility and presentation: Section 3.2 specifies Leg-T for selective copying, whereas Appendix C.2 specifies Leg-S. Appendix C.3 defines 12 possible value tokens, but the approximately 33% chance level asserted for associative recall is unexplained. Baseline architecture details, repeated-run uncertainty for Tables 1, 3, and 4, and forecasting rank and covariance regularization are insufficiently specified. These omissions and inconsistencies prevent confident reconstruction of the reported experiments.

Originality: Several constructions closely resemble established techniques: polynomial Volterra readouts, scalar time warping, normalized delta-rule associative updates, and reduced-rank linear prediction. New understanding can constitute a contribution, but the related-work discussion does not adequately establish what the polynomial formulation adds beyond these connections, especially for associative memory and forecast-induced geometry.

Significance and evidential scope: The short synthetic episodes and illustrative forecasting plots establish selected behaviors but provide limited evidence of robust long-range performance or practical interpretability benefits. Forecasting lacks quantitative held-out errors and sensitivity to the approximate delay used for training. Conversely, Appendix F's claim that continuous addressing is 'fundamentally mismatched' to language prediction is stronger than one small-model experiment supports. The negative result is valuable; the categorical inference is not.

strengths: Originality: The unifying perspective of explicit polynomial memories is appealing. Salience-induced history measures, polynomial associative storage, and forecast-dependent history geometry provide useful ways to inspect mechanisms that are harder to interpret in learned SSMs.
Soundness: The salience time-change derivation in Equations (2)–(5), minimum-norm associative write update, and linear predictive metric Q = TᵀWT have clear mathematical foundations.

Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, and the memory visualizations make the proposed mechanisms concrete. Figures 2, 3, and 5 are particularly helpful for understanding what the models retain and retrieve.

Significance and limitations: The reported synthetic-task successes suggest potential value for specialized, interpretable streaming models. The authors appropriately disclose weaker language-modeling performance, computational trade-offs, and the equivalence of multiscale dynamics to a bank of systems. These disclosures are strengths; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—foundational dynamics: Table 2's Leg-T matrix is inconsistent with its claimed uniform finite-window polynomial representation. Its first row gives ṡ₀ = −s₀ + f, independently of all higher coefficients, so s₀ is an exponential average rather than the uniform-window average, whose derivative is f(t) − f(t−1). Increasing the polynomial order cannot fix this discrepancy. Since several constructions and decoding interpretations depend on Leg-T, the paper must establish whether this is a table error or an implementation error and verify the affected results.

Soundness—finite-dimensional approximations: Appendix D.1 asserts gℓ(g) = Cℓ(g) for a finite polynomial vector, although multiplication raises the highest degree and requires a projection or residual. Similarly, exp(J_M) in Appendix D.3 is generally not the exact Galerkin matrix of multiplication by exp(u); truncation and exponentiation do not commute. The construction can be meaningful as an approximation, but the manuscript needs to identify that approximation and validate its effect on the claimed coefficient interpretation.

Evaluation—baseline fairness: The strongest comparative claims rely on inadequately configured baselines. Appendix C.6 indicates that the principal Transformer baselines omit positional embeddings, while Table 3 reports 99.7% associative-recall accuracy for a 27k-parameter, two-layer Transformer with positional embeddings and twice the training steps. This materially qualifies the main-text claim that baselines fail completely. Mamba is also absent from the selective-copying and associative-recall comparisons despite motivating those mechanisms. Parameter matching alone does not establish efficiency without accounting for recurrent-state size and computation.

Evaluation—multiscale efficiency: Appendix C.4 gives Multiscale HiPPO 16 × 128 = 2,048 state coefficients, versus 16 per single-scale comparator and 64 across the four listed comparators. Figure 4 therefore does not establish parsimonious memory or an advantage at matched storage. A matched-state bank with an appropriate horizon-query rule is especially important because Appendix D.4 explicitly establishes the bank equivalence.

Reproducibility: The appendix provides substantial detail but contains material inconsistencies. Section 3.2 specifies Leg-T for selective copying whereas Appendix C.2 specifies Leg-S. Appendix C.3 specifies 12 possible value tokens, while the results describe approximately 33% as chance without explaining the candidate set. Code-availability statements contain no usable link, Tables 1 and 4 omit run variability, and the forecasting rank and precise predictive-memory projector are not specified. These gaps prevent confident reconstruction of the reported experiments.

Originality and significance: The associative update is a normalized delta-rule memory using polynomial address features, but the related-work discussion does not adequately distinguish it from existing fast-weight and delta-rule memories. More generally, the synthetic demonstrations establish useful behaviors more clearly than broad advances: selective copying uses length-30 episodes, associative recall uses length-12 episodes, and forecasting is primarily illustrated qualitatively. Capacity, interference, length generalization, and quantitative forecasting studies would better establish the contribution's reach. The promising interpretability perspective does not outweigh the unresolved mathematical and evaluation issues in the current submission.
